claim: Dietary restriction increases the longevity of many organisms.
source: Dietary restriction increases the longevity of many organisms, but the cell signaling and organellar mechanisms underlying this capability are unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that references established scientific knowledge about dietary restriction and longevity.

claim: Yeast cells activate lipid-droplet consumption through micro-lipophagy (µ-lipophagy) to permit long-term survival in response to sudden glucose depletion.
source: We demonstrate that to permit long-term survival in response to sudden glucose depletion, yeast cells activate lipid-droplet (LD) consumption through micro-lipophagy (µ-lipophagy), in which fat is metabolized as an alternative energy source.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: AMPK activation triggers µ-lipophagy.
source: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation triggered this pathway, which required Atg14p.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that AMPK-deficient cells do not undergo µ-lipophagy.

claim: µ-lipophagy requires Atg14p.
source: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation triggered this pathway, which required Atg14p.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that atg14Δ cells fail to undergo µ-lipophagy.

claim: More gradual glucose starvation, amino acid deprivation or rapamycin did not trigger µ-lipophagy.
source: More gradual glucose starvation, amino acid deprivation or rapamycin did not trigger µ-lipophagy and failed to provide the needed substitute energy source for long-term survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different starvation conditions.

claim: Gradual glucose starvation, amino acid deprivation or rapamycin treatment failed to provide the needed substitute energy source for long-term survival.
source: More gradual glucose starvation, amino acid deprivation or rapamycin did not trigger µ-lipophagy and failed to provide the needed substitute energy source for long-term survival.
evidence: This is supported by cell survival data under different starvation conditions.

claim: During acute glucose restriction, activated AMPK was stabilized from degradation.
source: During acute glucose restriction, activated AMPK was stabilized from degradation and interacted with Atg14p.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing sustained AMPK phosphorylation under acute GR and proteasome inhibitor experiments.

claim: During acute glucose restriction, activated AMPK interacted with Atg14p.
source: During acute glucose restriction, activated AMPK was stabilized from degradation and interacted with Atg14p.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments showing interaction between Snf1p-HA and Atg14p.

claim: Atg14p redistributes from ER exit sites onto liquid-ordered vacuole membrane domains during acute glucose restriction.
source: This prompted Atg14p redistribution from ER exit sites onto liquid-ordered vacuole membrane domains, initiating µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data showing Atg14p localization changes under different starvation conditions.

claim: Atg14p redistribution onto liquid-ordered vacuole membrane domains initiates µ-lipophagy.
source: This prompted Atg14p redistribution from ER exit sites onto liquid-ordered vacuole membrane domains, initiating µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Atg14p localization to the vacuole correlates with µ-lipophagy induction.

claim: Nutrient-depleted cells can only persist long-term by initiating a two-pronged survival response: recycling cytoplasmic components and having a source of energy available from within the cell.
source: Nutrient-depleted cells can only persist long-term by initiating a two-pronged survival response: they need to be able to recycle cytoplasmic components and they need a source of energy available from within the cell.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about cellular survival mechanisms.

claim: Recycling of cytoplasmic components is achieved through self-digestion involving bulk autophagy pathways.
source: The first is achieved through self-digestion involving bulk autophagy pathways (Green et al., 2011; Yen and Klionsky, 2008), and the second requires a shift to metabolizing lipids for ATP production given the unavailability of glucose (Hardie and Carling, 1997; Zechner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Energy production in starved cells requires a shift to metabolizing lipids for ATP production given the unavailability of glucose.
source: The first is achieved through self-digestion involving bulk autophagy pathways (Green et al., 2011; Yen and Klionsky, 2008), and the second requires a shift to metabolizing lipids for ATP production given the unavailability of glucose (Hardie and Carling, 1997; Zechner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Caloric restriction and enhanced lifespan in various organisms are related.
source: Its answer is particularly relevant to aging research as caloric restriction and enhanced lifespan in various organisms are related (Cantó and Auwerx, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Not all caloric restriction programs have the same beneficial effects on organismal health and survival.
source: But not all caloric restriction programs have the same beneficial effects on organismal health and survival (Greer and Brunet, 2009; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Yeast cells starved by different nutrient regimes either die quickly or live long-term.
source: For example, yeast cells starved by different nutrient regimes either die quickly or live long-term (Goldberg et al., 2009); mice strains with differing sensitivities to different nutrients show variable responses to caloric restriction (Liao et al., 2010); and non-human primates exhibit short or long lifespans on different starvation diets (Colman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice strains with differing sensitivities to different nutrients show variable responses to caloric restriction.
source: For example, yeast cells starved by different nutrient regimes either die quickly or live long-term (Goldberg et al., 2009); mice strains with differing sensitivities to different nutrients show variable responses to caloric restriction (Liao et al., 2010); and non-human primates exhibit short or long lifespans on different starvation diets (Colman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-human primates exhibit short or long lifespans on different starvation diets.
source: For example, yeast cells starved by different nutrient regimes either die quickly or live long-term (Goldberg et al., 2009); mice strains with differing sensitivities to different nutrients show variable responses to caloric restriction (Liao et al., 2010); and non-human primates exhibit short or long lifespans on different starvation diets (Colman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells mount distinct survival responses depending on the starvation condition.
source: These results raise the possibility that cells mount distinct survival responses depending on the starvation condition, with only some regimens activating both lipid catabolism and autophagy, which are necessary for long-term survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited examples of variable responses to different starvation conditions.

claim: Only some starvation regimens activate both lipid catabolism and autophagy, which are necessary for long-term survival.
source: These results raise the possibility that cells mount distinct survival responses depending on the starvation condition, with only some regimens activating both lipid catabolism and autophagy, which are necessary for long-term survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited examples and is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Different regimens of depleting glucose during starvation lead to dramatically different cellular lifespans in budding yeast.
source: Prior work in budding yeast has shown that different regimens of depleting glucose during starvation lead to dramatically different cellular lifespans (Aris et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cells shifted into 0.4% glucose with no nutrient replenishment (acute glucose restriction) survive significantly longer than those placed in similar media containing 2% glucose (gradual glucose restriction).
source: In particular, cells growing in synthetic minimal (SD) media (containing a restricted set of amino acids) with 2% glucose that are shifted into 0.4% glucose with no nutrient replenishment (i.e. acute glucose restriction, Acute GR) survive significantly longer than those placed in similar media containing 2% glucose (i.e. gradual glucose restriction, Gradual GR), even though a majority of nutrients become completely depleted within 1 day under both conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the cell survival data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: ~99.9% of cells starved by gradual GR die within 9 days.
source: This surprising effect is shown in Figure 1A, with ~99.9% of cells starved by gradual GR dying within 9 days and nearly all cells starved by acute GR still alive after 25 days (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing cell survival data.

claim: Nearly all cells starved by acute GR are still alive after 25 days.
source: This surprising effect is shown in Figure 1A, with ~99.9% of cells starved by gradual GR dying within 9 days and nearly all cells starved by acute GR still alive after 25 days (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing cell survival data.

claim: By day 1 of GR, acutely-restricted cells had amplified their oxygen consumption rates to 2.2X that of gradually restricted cells.
source: By day 1 of GR, acutely-restricted cells had amplified their oxygen consumption rates to 2.2X that of gradually restricted cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing cell respiration data.

claim: Acutely restricted cells maintained higher respiratory rates after day 1, whereas gradually restricted cells exhibited a negligible oxygen consumption rate by day 3.
source: Thereafter, acutely restricted cells maintained this higher respiratory rate, whereas gradually restricted cells exhibited a negligible oxygen consumption rate by day 3.
evidence: This is supported by the cell respiration data in Figure 1B.

claim: Only cells undergoing acute GR remained viable after exposure to different oxidative stressors (hydrogen peroxide and menadione).
source: We also investigated the effect of oxidative stress on long-term cell viability under acute or gradual GR. Only cells undergoing acute GR remained viable after exposure to different oxidative stressors (i.e. hydrogen peroxide and menadione) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), with their viability resembling that of cells undergoing acute GR without stressors.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells undergoing acute GR for 3 days had highly fused and elaborate mitochondria.
source: Examining mitochondria morphology next, we observed that cells undergoing acute GR for 3 days had highly fused and elaborate mitochondria, whereas those undergoing gradual GR had exceedingly fragmented mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Cells undergoing gradual GR had exceedingly fragmented mitochondria.
source: Examining mitochondria morphology next, we observed that cells undergoing acute GR for 3 days had highly fused and elaborate mitochondria, whereas those undergoing gradual GR had exceedingly fragmented mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Cells genetically modified so they could not form LDs died quickly under glucose starvation.
source: In studying this response, we found that cells genetically modified so they could not form LDs died quickly under glucose starvation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; also see [Velázquez et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and a citation.

claim: Cells without vacuolar lipases had reduced survival rates under GR.
source: Moreover, cells without vacuolar lipases had reduced survival rates under GR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; also see [van Zutphen et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and a citation.

claim: Metabolic reprogramming for long-term survival under glucose starvation requires the activities of LDs and the vacuole.
source: These results suggested that metabolic reprogramming for long-term survival under glucose starvation requires the activities of LDs and the vacuole.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that cells lacking LDs or vacuolar lipases have reduced survival.

claim: In non-starved cells, LDs were exclusively localized in the cytoplasm, with none appearing within the vacuole.
source: In non-starved cells imaged using SXT, LDs (appearing as black spherical structures) were exclusively localized in the cytoplasm, with none appearing within the vacuole (Figure 1C, Non-starvation).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing SXT images.

claim: In cells undergoing gradual GR, LDs were mainly localized in the cytoplasm.
source: A similar cytoplasmic location was observed for LDs in cells undergoing gradual GR (Figure 1D and Video 1, Gradual GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: In cells starved by acute GR, LDs were observed in both the cytoplasm and vacuole.
source: By contrast, in cells starved by acute GR, LDs were observed in both the cytoplasm and vacuole (Figure 1D and Video 2, Acute GR); those in the vacuole appeared to have been engulfed as whole droplets.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D and Video 2.

claim: LDs in the vacuole of cells undergoing acute GR appeared to have been engulfed as whole droplets.
source: By contrast, in cells starved by acute GR, LDs were observed in both the cytoplasm and vacuole (Figure 1D and Video 2, Acute GR); those in the vacuole appeared to have been engulfed as whole droplets.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D and Video 2.

claim: Approximately 60% of cells starved by acute GR contained vacuole-localized LDs.
source: Quantification of the images revealed that approximately 60% of cells starved by acute GR contained vacuole-localized LDs compared to only ~10% of cells starved by gradual GR and none of non-starved cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E showing quantification data.

claim: Only ~10% of cells starved by gradual GR contained vacuole-localized LDs.
source: Quantification of the images revealed that approximately 60% of cells starved by acute GR contained vacuole-localized LDs compared to only ~10% of cells starved by gradual GR and none of non-starved cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E showing quantification data.

claim: Under acute GR cells quickly activate a cellular response pathway involving LD delivery into the vacuole, where LDs are digested to fuel mitochondrial OXPHOS.
source: These results suggested that under acute GR cells quickly activate a cellular response pathway involving LD delivery into the vacuole, where LDs are digested to fuel mitochondrial OXPHOS.
evidence: This is inferred from the SXT data showing LDs in the vacuole under acute GR and the increased oxygen consumption.

claim: Virtually no LDs were found inside the vacuole of atg1Δ or atg8Δ cells at 1.5 days of acute GR.
source: Virtually, no LDs were found inside the vacuole of atg1Δ or atg8Δ cells at 1.5 days of acute GR, in contrast to wild-type (WT) cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 2A, top panel, see quantification in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A and 2B showing SXT images and quantification.

claim: LD accumulation within the vacuole during acute GR occurs by autophagy.
source: This indicated that LD accumulation within the vacuole during acute GR occurs by autophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that autophagy-deficient cells (atg1Δ and atg8Δ) do not accumulate LDs in the vacuole.

claim: LDs are directly engulfed by the vacuole by a micro-autophagy mechanism during acute GR.
source: During this process, LDs appeared to be directly engulfed by the vacuole by a micro-autophagy mechanism, as previously reported (van Zutphen et al., 2014; Vevea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the SXT images and citations to prior literature.

claim: WT cells undergoing acute GR had ~50% less total LD volume relative to the cells undergoing gradual GR.
source: First, WT cells undergoing acute GR had ~50% less total LD volume relative to the cells undergoing gradual GR, with most LD volume in the vacuole; and, this reduction in total LD volume was absent in atg1Δ cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C showing LD volume quantification.

claim: The reduction in total LD volume under acute GR was absent in atg1Δ cells.
source: First, WT cells undergoing acute GR had ~50% less total LD volume relative to the cells undergoing gradual GR, with most LD volume in the vacuole; and, this reduction in total LD volume was absent in atg1Δ cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C showing LD volume quantification.

claim: Within 3 days of starvation, WT cells under acute GR produced high levels of free DsRed, indicative of LD turnover.
source: Second, Western blot analysis of cells expressing the LD marker Erg6-DsRed revealed that within 3 days of starvation, WT cells under acute GR produced high levels of free DsRed, indicative of LD turnover, whereas similarly starved atg1Δ cells did not (Figure 2D, Acute GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D showing Western blot data.

claim: atg1Δ cells under acute GR did not produce high levels of free DsRed within 3 days of starvation.
source: Second, Western blot analysis of cells expressing the LD marker Erg6-DsRed revealed that within 3 days of starvation, WT cells under acute GR produced high levels of free DsRed, indicative of LD turnover, whereas similarly starved atg1Δ cells did not (Figure 2D, Acute GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D showing Western blot data.

claim: Virtually no free DsRed was released from cells undergoing gradual GR in WT or atg1Δ cells.
source: Virtually, no free DsRed was released from cells undergoing gradual GR in WT or atg1Δ cells (Figure 2D, Gradual GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D showing Western blot data.

claim: Confocal imaging of Erg6-DsRed-expressing cells showed DsRed signal dispersed inside the vacuole between day 1 and day 3 of acute GR.
source: Finally, confocal imaging of Erg6-DsRed-expressing cells showed DsRed signal dispersed inside the vacuole between day 1 and day 3 of acute GR (Figure 2E, see arrowheads), whereas DsRed signal was associated with cytoplasmic puncta in either atg1Δ cells or cells starved by gradual GR.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E showing confocal images.

claim: DsRed signal was associated with cytoplasmic puncta in either atg1Δ cells or cells starved by gradual GR.
source: Finally, confocal imaging of Erg6-DsRed-expressing cells showed DsRed signal dispersed inside the vacuole between day 1 and day 3 of acute GR (Figure 2E, see arrowheads), whereas DsRed signal was associated with cytoplasmic puncta in either atg1Δ cells or cells starved by gradual GR.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E showing confocal images.

claim: The µ-lipophagy triggered by acute GR leads to LD turnover in these cells.
source: Thus, the µ-lipophagy triggered by acute GR leads to LD turnover in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing LD volume reduction and free DsRed release under acute GR.

claim: Autophagic flux was maintained long-term under acute GR but not under gradual GR.
source: Examining overall autophagy rates using GFP release from GFP-Atg8 revealed that autophagic flux was maintained long-term under acute GR but not under gradual GR (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2F showing Western blot data.

claim: Cells that sense acute GR can initiate and maintain both µ-lipophagy and bulk autophagy pathways for long-term survival under complete nutrient deprivation.
source: It is cells that sense acute GR, therefore, that can initiate and maintain both µ-lipophagy and bulk autophagy pathways for long-term survival under complete nutrient deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing sustained autophagic flux and µ-lipophagy under acute GR.

claim: Replacing SD media with SC media (which contains excess amino acids) did not significantly change the management of autophagy and LDs under acute or gradual GR.
source: To address this possibility, we replaced SD media (which lacks a majority of amino acids) with synthetic complete (SC) media, which contains excess amino acids. No significant change in the management of autophagy and LDs under acute or gradual GR occurred by this media switch (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A and B showing flux assay data.

claim: Amino acid depletion is not a major factor in triggering µ-lipophagy during acute GR.
source: This suggested amino acid depletion is not a major factor in triggering µ-lipophagy during acute GR.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that adding amino acids does not affect µ-lipophagy under acute GR.

claim: Rapamycin treatment of cells undergoing gradual GR led to a transient increase in autophagic flux.
source: Rapamycin treatment of cells undergoing gradual GR led to a transient increase in autophagic flux (Figure 3C, gradual GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C showing flux assay data.

claim: The autophagy induced by rapamycin in cells undergoing gradual GR could not be maintained and declined within 1 day.
source: This was as expected given inactivated TOR's role in triggering autophagy. However, the autophagy could not be maintained and declined within 1 day.
evidence: This is supported by the flux assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: LD degradation in rapamycin-treated cells under gradual GR remained low.
source: Notably, LD degradation (assessed using Erg6-DsRed) in rapamycin-treated cells under gradual GR remained low (Figure 3D, Gradual GR), similar to cells under gradual GR not treated with rapamycin (see Gradual GR in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D showing LD flux assay data.

claim: TOR inactivation by rapamycin in cells undergoing gradual GR does not induce long-term autophagic flux or µ-lipophagy.
source: This showed that TOR inactivation by rapamycin in cells undergoing gradual GR does not induce long-term autophagic flux or µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing transient autophagy and no µ-lipophagy with rapamycin treatment under gradual GR.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not substantially boost general autophagic flux in cells undergoing acute GR.
source: We next examined the effect of rapamycin treatment on cells undergoing acute GR. No substantial boost occurred in general autophagic flux (Figure 3C, Acute GR) compared to untreated cells undergoing acute GR (see Figure 3A, Acute GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C showing flux assay data.

claim: LD degradation was decreased by rapamycin treatment in cells undergoing acute GR.
source: However, LD degradation was surprisingly decreased (Figure 3D, Acute GR) relative to untreated cells undergoing acute GR (see Figure 3B, Acute GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D showing LD flux assay data.

claim: Inactivation of the amino-acid-sensing TOR system during acute GR blocks µ-lipophagy rather than promotes it.
source: This suggested that inactivation of the amino-acid-sensing TOR system during acute GR blocks µ-lipophagy rather than promotes it.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing decreased LD degradation with rapamycin treatment under acute GR.

claim: The high levels of LD degradation characteristic of acute GR in WT cells were not seen in snf1Δ or snf4Δ cells undergoing acute GR.
source: The high levels of LD degradation (assessed by release of free DsRed from Erg6-DsRed) characteristic of acute GR in WT cells were not seen in snf1Δ or snf4Δ cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 3E, Acute GR), and instead resembled that of WT, snf1Δ, or snf4Δ cells when undergoing gradual GR (Figure 3E, Gradual GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E showing LD flux assay data.

claim: LD consumption seen under acute GR requires AMPK activity.
source: LD consumption seen under acute GR thus appears to require AMPK activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that AMPK-deficient cells do not degrade LDs under acute GR.

claim: When snf1Δ and snf4Δ cells were starved by acute GR for 3 days, no DsRed signal inside the vacuole was seen by confocal imaging.
source: When snf1Δ and snf4Δ cells were labeled with Erg6-DsRed and Vph1-GFP (a vacuole membrane marker) and starved by acute GR for 3 days, no DsRed signal inside the vacuole was seen by confocal imaging, in contrast to similarly-starved WT cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3F showing confocal images.

claim: LDs were excluded from the vacuole in snf1Δ cells after 1.5 days of acute GR.
source: Examination of snf1Δ cells by SXT after 1.5 days of acute GR revealed LDs were excluded from the vacuole, in contrast to WT cells undergoing acute GR, where LDs were readily taken up (Figure 3G, black arrows point to LDs).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3G showing SXT images.

claim: LDs in snf1Δ cells had an overall larger size and the total LD volume in these cells was increased relative to WT cells undergoing acute GR.
source: Examining full 3D SXT tomograms showed that LDs in snf1Δ cells had an overall larger size and that the total LD volume in these cells was increased relative to WT cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), as expected if µ-lipophagy was not induced.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Autophagic bodies, but not LDs, could be seen inside the vacuole in SXT images of snf1Δ cells starved by acute GR.
source: Autophagic bodies (ABs), but not LDs, could be seen inside the vacuole in SXT images of snf1Δ cells starved by acute GR (Figure 3G, white arrows point to these ABs, which are less dense than LDs because they contain fluid portions of the cytoplasm with less lipid [Tsukada and Ohsumi, 1993]).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3G showing SXT images and a citation.

claim: µ-lipophagy, not bulk autophagy, is preferentially inhibited when AMPK is absent from cells starved by acute GR.
source: This suggested that µ-lipophagy, not bulk autophagy, is preferentially inhibited when AMPK is absent from cells starved by acute GR.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing autophagic bodies but not LDs in the vacuole of snf1Δ cells.

claim: Total autophagic flux decreased but was not completely abolished in snf1Δ or snf4Δ cells undergoing acute GR relative to similarly starved WT cells.
source: Supporting this, total autophagic flux (measured using GFP release from GFP-Atg8) decreased but was not completely abolished in snf1Δ or snf4Δ cells undergoing acute GR relative to similarly starved WT cells (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AMPK-deficient cells (snf1Δ cells) had significantly reduced ATP levels under acute GR.
source: In addition to µ-lipophagy being blocked in AMPK-deficient cells (i.e. snf1Δ cells), these cells had significantly reduced ATP levels and shortened lifespans under acute GR, resembling cells undergoing gradual GR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AMPK-deficient cells (snf1Δ cells) had shortened lifespans under acute GR.
source: In addition to µ-lipophagy being blocked in AMPK-deficient cells (i.e. snf1Δ cells), these cells had significantly reduced ATP levels and shortened lifespans under acute GR, resembling cells undergoing gradual GR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Under acute GR, AMPK activation, µ-lipophagy, and downstream ATP generation are tightly linked for ensuring cell survival.
source: Under acute GR, therefore, AMPK activation, µ-lipophagy, and downstream ATP generation appear to be tightly linked for ensuring cell survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that AMPK-deficient cells have reduced µ-lipophagy, ATP levels, and survival.

claim: AMPK became active within 4 hr of acute GR.
source: Measuring Thr210 phosphorylation of Snf1p as indicator of AMPK activation (McCartney and Schmidt, 2001), we found AMPK became active within 4 hr of acute GR, whereas non-starved cells or cells undergoing gradual GR showed little AMPK activation at this time (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A showing Western blot data and a citation.

claim: Non-starved cells or cells undergoing gradual GR showed little AMPK activation at 4 hr.
source: Measuring Thr210 phosphorylation of Snf1p as indicator of AMPK activation (McCartney and Schmidt, 2001), we found AMPK became active within 4 hr of acute GR, whereas non-starved cells or cells undergoing gradual GR showed little AMPK activation at this time (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A showing Western blot data.

claim: AMPK activation remained low under gradual GR conditions when cells were incubated for 4 hr in media with rapamycin.
source: AMPK activation also remained low under gradual GR conditions when cells were incubated for 4 hr in media with rapamycin. This suggests that TOR inhibition also does not activate AMPK at this time point (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B showing Western blot data.

claim: TOR inhibition does not activate AMPK at 4 hr.
source: AMPK activation also remained low under gradual GR conditions when cells were incubated for 4 hr in media with rapamycin. This suggests that TOR inhibition also does not activate AMPK at this time point (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing low AMPK activation with rapamycin treatment.

claim: Under acute GR, phosphorylated Snf1p levels measurably increased after 18 hr and were maintained thereafter.
source: Under acute GR, phosphorylated Snf1p levels measurably increased after 18 hr and were maintained thereafter.
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Under gradual GR, significant levels of phosphorylated Snf1p were present at 18 hr, but the levels fell thereafter, becoming very low by 36 hr.
source: Under gradual GR, by contrast, significant levels of phosphorylated Snf1p were present at 18 hr, but the levels fell thereafter, becoming very low by 36 hr (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C showing Western blot data.

claim: Addition of the proteasome inhibitor MG132 to cells undergoing gradual GR at 18 hr increased total Snf1p levels at 24 hr and 36 hr.
source: Notably, addition of the proteasome inhibitor MG132 to these cells at 18 hr increased total Snf1p levels at 24 hr and 36 hr (Figure 4C), although by 36 hr the phosphorylated pool of Snf1p in total Snf1p was still decreased in cells undergoing gradual GR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C showing Western blot data.

claim: AMPK is activated only short-term under gradual GR because the protein and its phosphorylated form undergo rapid proteasomal degradation.
source: This suggested that AMPK is activated only short-term under gradual GR because the protein and its phosphorylated form undergo rapid proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that proteasome inhibition increases Snf1p levels under gradual GR.

claim: Under acute GR, Snf1p and its phosphorylated form are protected from degradation and therefore more stable.
source: By contrast, under acute GR, Snf1p and its phosphorylated form appear to be protected from degradation and therefore more stable.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing sustained Snf1p levels under acute GR.

claim: Loss of phosphorylated and total Snf1p was accelerated within 24 hr of acute GR when TOR was inhibited by rapamycin treatment.
source: Interestingly, loss of phosphorylated and total Snf1p was accelerated within 24 hr of acute GR when TOR was inhibited by rapamycin treatment (Figure 4E, Acute GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E showing Western blot data.

claim: Degradation of phosphorylated and total Snf1p sped up during gradual GR when rapamycin was present, with Snf1p no longer detectable at 24 hr treatment.
source: Degradation of phosphorylated and total Snf1p also sped up during gradual GR when rapamycin was present, with Snf1p no longer detectable at 24 hr treatment (Figure 4E, Gradual GR).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E showing Western blot data.

claim: Rapamycin treatment antagonizes AMPK activity.
source: This indicated rapamycin treatment antagonizes AMPK activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing accelerated Snf1p degradation with rapamycin treatment.

claim: Rapamycin treatment decreases µ-lipophagy under acute GR because µ-lipophagy depends on AMPK activation.
source: As µ-lipophagy depends on AMPK activation (see Figure 3E, Acute GR), this could explain why rapamycin treatment decreases µ-lipophagy under acute GR (see Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that rapamycin antagonizes AMPK and that AMPK is required for µ-lipophagy.

claim: Rapamycin treatment diminished cell viability in a dose-dependent manner under both acute and gradual GR conditions.
source: Rapamycin treatment diminished cell viability in a dose-dependent manner under both acute and gradual GR conditions (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A similar effect on cell viability was observed when amino acids were depleted from the media (SD gradual and SD acute GR).
source: A similar effect was observed when amino acids were depleted from the media (i.e., SD gradual and SD acute GR) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TOR inactivation is insufficient to keep cells alive under glucose restriction.
source: Therefore, TOR inactivation is insufficient to keep cells alive under glucose restriction, potentially because it inhibits long-term AMPK activation, which is necessary to maintain µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced cell viability with rapamycin treatment.

claim: Thirteen ATG genes known to be essential for general autophagy were also necessary for µ-lipophagy.
source: Thirteen ATG genes known to be essential for general autophagy were also necessary for µ-lipophagy; including genes for autophagosome induction (i.e. ATG1, ATG6, ATG13 and ATG14), maturation (i.e. ATG3, ATG5, ATG7, ATG10, ATG12 and ATG16), and membrane retrieval (i.e. ATG2, ATG9 and ATG18) (Nakatogawa et al., 2009) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing flux assay data and a citation.

claim: µ-lipophagy in cells undergoing acute GR depends on bona fide autophagosomal machinery.
source: This indicated that µ-lipophagy in cells undergoing acute GR depends on bona fide autophagosomal machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that core autophagy genes are required for µ-lipophagy.

claim: Four out of the 31 ATG genes functioned in µ-lipophagy without complete loss of autophagy activity in acutely glucose-restricted cells: ATG8, ATG14, ATG23, and ATG34.
source: We found that four out of the 31 ATG genes functioned in µ-lipophagy without complete loss of autophagy activity in acutely glucose-restricted cells: these were ATG8, ATG14, ATG23, and ATG34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing flux assay data.

claim: ATG14 is the candidate gene specifically required for µ-lipophagy under acute GR.
source: This left as our candidate gene ATG14 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the process of elimination described in the text and supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: Atg14p is a component of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) complex I, which is involved in autophagosomal membrane biogenesis.
source: Atg14p is known to be a component of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) complex I, which is involved in autophagosomal membrane biogenesis. It forms a complex with Atg6p to support the lipid kinase activity of Vps34p under nitrogen starvation (Araki et al., 2013; Obara and Ohsumi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Atg14p forms a complex with Atg6p to support the lipid kinase activity of Vps34p under nitrogen starvation.
source: Atg14p is known to be a component of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) complex I, which is involved in autophagosomal membrane biogenesis. It forms a complex with Atg6p to support the lipid kinase activity of Vps34p under nitrogen starvation (Araki et al., 2013; Obara and Ohsumi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Much less autophagic flux and fewer Atg8 punctate structures were observed in atg14Δ cells relative to WT cells under nitrogen starvation.
source: Consistent with this role, we observed much less autophagic flux (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and fewer Atg8 punctate structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C) in atg14Δ cells relative to WT cells under nitrogen starvation.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B, and C.

claim: Autophagic flux was inhibited in both atg1Δ and atg14Δ cells relative to WT cells when treated with rapamycin.
source: Additionally, when we treated cells expressing GFP-Atg8 with rapamycin and measured autophagic flux in WT, atg1Δ, or atg14Δ cells, autophagic flux was inhibited in both atg1Δ and atg14Δ cells relative to WT cells (with less inhibition in atg14Δ compared to atg1Δ cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Atg14p was not essential for general autophagic flux under acute GR.
source: In contrast to nitrogen starvation and rapamycin treatment, Atg14p was not essential for general autophagic flux under acute GR. GFP release from GFP-Atg8 (Figure 5A, GFP-Atg8 panel) or GFP-Pho8Δ60 (Figure 5B) still occurred in atg14Δ cells, decreasing only slightly compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A and 5B showing flux assay data.

claim: atg14Δ cells undergoing acute GR showed a significant block in LD degradation.
source: Despite this, atg14Δ cells undergoing acute GR showed a significant block in LD degradation (Figure 5A, Erg6-DsRed panel), implying Atg14p's role in cells undergoing acute GR is to drive µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A showing LD flux assay data.

claim: Atg14p's role in cells undergoing acute GR is to drive µ-lipophagy.
source: Despite this, atg14Δ cells undergoing acute GR showed a significant block in LD degradation (Figure 5A, Erg6-DsRed panel), implying Atg14p's role in cells undergoing acute GR is to drive µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that atg14Δ cells have reduced LD degradation but not general autophagy under acute GR.

claim: No Erg6-DsRed or LD structures redistributed into the vacuole in atg14Δ cells under acute GR.
source: We tested this hypothesis with confocal imaging of Erg6-DsRed and direct visualization of LDs using SXT in atg14Δ cells under acute GR. No Erg6-DsRed or LD structures redistributed into the vacuole in these cells (Figure 5C and D), supporting a role of Atg14p in initiating µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5C and D showing confocal and SXT images.

claim: Atg14p was not required for pexophagy.
source: By contrast, Atg14p was not required for pexophagy, the specialized form of autophagy involved in degrading peroxisomes (Suzuki, 2013): substantial degradation of the peroxisomal marker Pot1-GFP still occurred in atg14Δ cells under GR, whereas no Pot1-GFP degradation occurred in atg11Δ cells, where pexophagy is blocked (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F and a citation.

claim: ATG14 has been shown to be dispensable for autophagic degradation of ER components.
source: Given that ATG14 has also been shown to be dispensable for autophagic degradation of ER components (Schuck et al., 2014), we concluded Atg14p's role under acute GR is primarily to induce µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Atg14p's role under acute GR is primarily to induce µ-lipophagy.
source: Given that ATG14 has also been shown to be dispensable for autophagic degradation of ER components (Schuck et al., 2014), we concluded Atg14p's role under acute GR is primarily to induce µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Atg14p is not required for other autophagy pathways but is required for µ-lipophagy.

claim: atg14Δ cells under acute GR had less LD volume loss relative to that of WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR.
source: We found that atg14Δ cells under acute GR: had less LD volume loss relative to that of WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 5E); depleted their ATP levels significantly faster than WT cells (or pexophagy-deficient atg11Δ cells) under acute GR (Figure 5F); and had significantly shortened lifespans relative to WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5E showing LD volume data.

claim: atg14Δ cells depleted their ATP levels significantly faster than WT cells under acute GR.
source: We found that atg14Δ cells under acute GR: had less LD volume loss relative to that of WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 5E); depleted their ATP levels significantly faster than WT cells (or pexophagy-deficient atg11Δ cells) under acute GR (Figure 5F); and had significantly shortened lifespans relative to WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5F showing ATP level data.

claim: atg14Δ cells had significantly shortened lifespans relative to WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR.
source: We found that atg14Δ cells under acute GR: had less LD volume loss relative to that of WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 5E); depleted their ATP levels significantly faster than WT cells (or pexophagy-deficient atg11Δ cells) under acute GR (Figure 5F); and had significantly shortened lifespans relative to WT or atg11Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5G showing cell survival data.

claim: The shortened lifespan of atg14Δ cells under acute GR was similar to that seen for atg1Δ, atg5Δ, and atg23Δ cells, which lack core general autophagy machinery.
source: The shortened lifespan of atg14Δ cells under acute GR was similar to that seen for atg1Δ, atg5Δ, and atg23Δ cells, which lack core general autophagy machinery (see Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3A.

claim: Atg14p and other core autophagy machinery are critical for the energy metabolism and long-term survival of cells starved acutely of glucose.
source: Therefore, Atg14p and other core autophagy machinery are critical for the energy metabolism and long-term survival of cells starved acutely of glucose.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that atg14Δ cells have reduced ATP levels and shortened lifespans under acute GR.

claim: Other types of autophagy, including pexophagy (controlled by Atg11p) and mitophagy (controlled by Atg11p, Atg32p, and Atg33p), did not have a critical role in long-term survival under acute GR.
source: Other types of autophagy, including pexophagy (controlled by Atg11p) and mitophagy (controlled by Atg11p, Atg32p, and Atg33p), did not have this role (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Under gradual GR, atg14Δ cells displayed an almost identical lifespan as WT or atg11Δ cells, with the vast majority of these cells dead by 13 days.
source: Under gradual GR (in which µ-lipophagy is not induced), atg14Δ cells displayed an almost identical lifespan as WT or atg11Δ cells, with the vast majority of these cells dead by 13 days (>99.9%, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5G showing cell survival data.

claim: Atg14p's pro-survival role in starved cells is connected to its regulation of µ-lipophagy.
source: This suggested Atg14p's pro-survival role in starved cells is connected to its regulation of µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that atg14Δ cells have normal lifespans under gradual GR (where µ-lipophagy is not induced) but shortened lifespans under acute GR (where µ-lipophagy is induced).

claim: Under no GR or gradual GR, Atg14p was localized solely within the cytoplasm in a dispersed and/or punctate pattern.
source: Under no GR or gradual GR, Atg14p was localized solely within the cytoplasm in a dispersed and/or punctate pattern (Figure 6A and B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A, B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing confocal images.

claim: The punctate structures of Atg14p co-localized with Sec13p (a subunit of the COPII vesicle coat mediating ER-to-Golgi transport).
source: The punctate structures co-localized with Sec13p (a subunit of the COPII vesicle coat mediating ER-to-Golgi transport) (Figure 6C), supporting prior work implicating Atg14p in the formation of pre-autophagosomal structures at ER exit sites (ERES) under nitrogen starvation conditions (Graef et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6C showing confocal images and a citation.

claim: Atg14p in cells undergoing acute GR became highly enriched on the vacuole surface.
source: In contrast to this distribution, Atg14p in cells undergoing acute GR became highly enriched on the vacuole surface (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A-C showing confocal images.

claim: Atg14p failed to redistribute onto the vacuole surface and remained at ERES in snf1Δ cells undergoing acute GR.
source: Notably, Atg14p failed to redistribute onto the vacuole surface and remained at ERES in snf1Δ cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 6D), in which AMPK is absent and µ-lipophagy is inhibited.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6D showing confocal images.

claim: Re-introduction of Snf1p-HA into snf1Δ cells under acute GR led to Atg14p re-localizing onto the vacuole surface.
source: Re-introduction of Snf1p-HA into snf1Δ cells under acute GR led to Atg14p re-localizing onto the vacuole surface (Figure 6A and B), and reversed the growth defects seen in these cells under glucose starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A, B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under acute GR, Atg14p redistributes in an AMPK-dependent manner from ERES to vacuolar membranes where it helps to induce µ-lipophagy.
source: These results suggested that under acute GR, Atg14p redistributes in an AMPK-dependent manner from ERES to vacuolar membranes where it helps to induce µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Atg14p localization to the vacuole requires AMPK.

claim: Atg14p functions downstream of AMPK in the µ-lipophagy pathway.
source: Atg14p appeared to function downstream of AMPK in this pathway because atg14Δ cells did not prevent AMPK (i.e. Snf1p) from being phosphorylated under acute GR (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), whereas snf1Δ cells prevented Atg14p from re-localizing onto the vacuole (see above).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that AMPK is still activated in atg14Δ cells but Atg14p does not relocalize in snf1Δ cells.

claim: Atg14p did not relocate onto the vacuolar surface in rapamycin-treated cells undergoing acute GR.
source: Notably, Atg14p did not relocate onto the vacuolar surface in rapamycin-treated cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 6E–G); instead, it localized within cytoplasmic puncta that often co-localized with Sec13p (see arrowheads in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6E-G showing confocal images.

claim: Atg14p's localization to the vacuole under acute GR is antagonized by TOR inhibition (rapamycin treatment).
source: Thus, Atg14p's localization to the vacuole under acute GR is antagonized by TOR inhibition (i.e. rapamycin treatment).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that rapamycin prevents Atg14p from localizing to the vacuole under acute GR.

claim: Atg14p interacts with Snf1p-HA upon acute GR.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments using cells harboring a Snf1p-HA plasmid and GFP-tagged Atg14p revealed Atg14p interacts with Snf1p-HA upon acute GR, in contrast to another autophagy-related PI3K component, Atg6p (Obara and Ohsumi, 2011), which did not significantly interact with Snf1p compared to Atg14p (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3B showing immunoprecipitation data and a citation.

claim: Atg6p did not significantly interact with Snf1p compared to Atg14p upon acute GR.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments using cells harboring a Snf1p-HA plasmid and GFP-tagged Atg14p revealed Atg14p interacts with Snf1p-HA upon acute GR, in contrast to another autophagy-related PI3K component, Atg6p (Obara and Ohsumi, 2011), which did not significantly interact with Snf1p compared to Atg14p (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3B showing immunoprecipitation data.

claim: AMPK and Atg14p coexist in a complex under acute GR conditions.
source: AMPK and Atg14p therefore appear to coexist in a complex under acute GR conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between Snf1p and Atg14p.

claim: Atg6p remained localized on the vacuole surface after shifting to either acute or gradual GR.
source: Prior to glucose starvation, Atg6p and Vps15p both showed significant association with the vacuole surface. Whereas Atg6p remained localized there after shifting to either acute or gradual GR, Vps15p redistributed off the vacuole upon acute GR (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7A and B showing confocal images.

claim: Vps15p redistributed off the vacuole upon acute GR.
source: Prior to glucose starvation, Atg6p and Vps15p both showed significant association with the vacuole surface. Whereas Atg6p remained localized there after shifting to either acute or gradual GR, Vps15p redistributed off the vacuole upon acute GR (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7A and B showing confocal images.

claim: Atg38p, Vps34p, and Vps38p remained primarily cytosolic with no increased vacuolar association upon shift to either acute or gradual GR.
source: The other PI3K complex I components (i.e. Atg38p, Vps34p, and Vps38p) remained primarily cytosolic with no increased vacuolar association upon shift to either acute or gradual GR (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7A and B showing confocal images.

claim: Only Atg6p and Atg14p reside on the vacuole surface under acute GR, potentially serving as important initiators of µ-lipophagy.
source: This meant that only Atg6p and Atg14p reside on the vacuole surface under acute GR, potentially serving as important initiators of µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that only Atg6p and Atg14p localize to the vacuole under acute GR.

claim: Only Atg14p's vacuolar localization was AMPK-dependent.
source: In addition, only Atg14p's vacuolar localization was AMPK-dependent, since Atg6p remained prominently localized at the vacuolar surface even when AMPK was inactive (i.e. in snf1Δ cells or during gradual GR) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7C showing confocal images.

claim: When budding yeast are starved of glucose, they form distinct sterol-enriched, liquid-ordered (Lo) domains and liquid-disordered membrane (Ld) domains on their vacuolar surface.
source: Prior work has shown that when budding yeast are starved of glucose, they form distinct sterol-enriched, liquid-ordered (Lo) domains and liquid-disordered membrane (Ld) domains on their vacuolar surface (Toulmay and Prinz, 2013), with the Lo domains serving as preferential internalization sites for LDs (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lo domains serve as preferential internalization sites for LDs.
source: Prior work has shown that when budding yeast are starved of glucose, they form distinct sterol-enriched, liquid-ordered (Lo) domains and liquid-disordered membrane (Ld) domains on their vacuolar surface (Toulmay and Prinz, 2013), with the Lo domains serving as preferential internalization sites for LDs (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Large, marker-free Lo domains were observed on the vacuole membrane in cells undergoing acute GR.
source: Using GFP-Pho8 as a marker for Ld domains, we observed large, marker-free Lo domains on the vacuole membrane in cells undergoing acute GR (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8A showing confocal images.

claim: LDs resided exclusively in the Lo domains in cells undergoing acute GR.
source: LDs, labeled using Erg6-DsRed, resided exclusively in the Lo domains, consistent with the Lo domains serving as preferential sites for LD uptake into the vacuole.
evidence: This is supported by the confocal images in Figure 8A.

claim: In cells undergoing gradual GR, Lo domains were much less apparent, and LDs were mainly clustered near one side of the vacuole.
source: By contrast, in cells undergoing gradual GR, Lo domains were much less apparent, and LDs were mainly clustered near one side of the vacuole (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8B showing confocal images.

claim: Acute GR drives both the formation of large Lo domains on the vacuole membrane and LD association with these domains.
source: Acute GR therefore appears to drive both the formation of large Lo domains on the vacuole membrane and LD association with these domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing large Lo domains and LD association with them under acute GR.

claim: Atg14p molecules localize as punctate elements within vacuolar Lo domains under acute GR.
source: 3D volume reconstruction and maximum projection images revealed Atg14p molecules localizing as punctate elements within vacuolar Lo domains (Video 3 and Figure 8C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Video 3 and Figure 8C showing AIRY-scan confocal images.

claim: Atg14p was preferentially localized on the edges of Lo domains.
source: Single z-slices from these images showed Atg14p was preferentially localized on the edges of Lo domains (Figure 8C, Single z-slice), in close association with LDs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atg6p localized in Lo domains at the vacuole surface but was more broadly distributed relative to Atg14p.
source: Atg6p also localized in Lo domains at the vacuole surface but was more broadly distributed relative to Atg14p (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8D showing AIRY-scan confocal images.

claim: Little or no Lo domains were observed in either atg14Δ or atg6Δ cells under acute or gradual GR.
source: To address whether Atg14p and/or Atg6p are critical for creating the large Lo domains on vacuole membranes under acute GR, we deleted the gene for each protein and then examined whether or not Lo domains were formed. Little or no Lo domains were observed in either atg14Δ or atg6Δ cells under acute or gradual GR, with the effect most potent in atg6Δ cells (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8E and F showing confocal images.

claim: Atg14p triggers large-scale Lo formation under acute GR, with a critical supportive role played by Atg6p.
source: Given that Atg6p resides on the vacuole membrane irrespective of the starvation condition (see Figure 7C), the results suggested Atg14p triggers large-scale Lo formation under acute GR, with a critical supportive role played by Atg6p.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that both Atg14p and Atg6p are required for Lo domain formation.

claim: Fewer large-scale Lo domains formed in snf1Δ cells under acute GR.
source: Consistent with this, fewer large-scale Lo domains formed in snf1Δ cells under acute GR (Figure 8E and F), a condition where Atg6p resides on the vacuole surface but Atg14p is not recruited there (see Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8E and F showing confocal images.

claim: For cells to survive long-term under full nutrient starvation, they need AMPK/Snf1p to be activated and stabilized.
source: We found that for cells to survive long-term under full nutrient starvation, they need AMPK/Snf1p, the cell's major ATP sensor, to be activated and stabilized.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: AMPK activation and stabilization occurred when cells sensed an acute depletion of glucose at the beginning of starvation.
source: This occurred when cells sensed an acute depletion of glucose at the beginning of starvation (i.e. acute GR).
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data showing sustained AMPK phosphorylation under acute GR.

claim: AMPK activation induced the pathways for µ-lipophagy, general autophagy, OXPHOS and stress resistance necessary for long-term survival.
source: This induced the pathways for µ-lipophagy, general autophagy, OXPHOS and stress resistance necessary for long-term survival.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing increased µ-lipophagy, autophagy, oxygen consumption, and stress resistance under acute GR.

claim: All these pathways (µ-lipophagy, general autophagy, OXPHOS and stress resistance) were attenuated and cellular lifespan shortened in cells lacking AMPK activity (snf1Δ cells).
source: In contrast, all these pathways were attenuated and cellular lifespan shortened in cells lacking AMPK activity (i.e. snf1Δ cells).
evidence: This is supported by the data showing reduced µ-lipophagy, autophagy, ATP levels, and survival in snf1Δ cells.

claim: AMPK acts as a critical upstream regulator of yeast cell survival under starvation.
source: The finding that AMPK acts as a critical upstream regulator of yeast cell survival under starvation supports prior work in C. elegans similarly implicating AMPK's role in lifespan extension under dietary restriction (Greer et al., 2007; Schulz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript and citations to prior literature.

claim: Rapamycin treatment or gradual GR did not maintain AMPK activity once it was switched on, and resulted in shortened cellular lifespans.
source: Other nutrient depletion conditions besides acute GR, including rapamycin treatment or gradual GR, did not maintain AMPK activity once it was switched on, and resulted in shortened cellular lifespans.
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data showing transient AMPK activation and cell survival data.

claim: TOR is inhibited early on by rapamycin treatment or gradual GR, which would induce bulk autophagy and cause a surplus in amino acids, raising ATP levels to antagonize AMPK activity.
source: We speculate this effect arose because TOR is inhibited early on by these treatments: this would induce bulk autophagy and cause a surplus in amino acids, raising ATP levels to antagonize AMPK activity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Gradual GR causes cells to sense amino acid depletion before glucose reduction from the medium, leading to TOR inhibition and its prevention of AMPK activation.
source: While rapamycin treatment directly inhibits TOR, gradual GR would do so by causing cells to sense amino acid depletion before glucose reduction from the medium, leading to TOR inhibition and its prevention of AMPK activation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: mTOR inhibition activates overall protein degradation by the ubiquitin proteasome system.
source: However, prior work has demonstrated that mTOR inhibition activates overall protein degradation by the ubiquitin proteasome system (Zhao et al., 2015), and we found that both rapamycin and gradual GR treatments caused proteasomal degradation of AMPK (in contrast to acute GR treatment, which resulted in long-term AMPK activation).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and the proteasome inhibitor experiments in the manuscript.

claim: A key survival promoting role of AMPK under acute GR is the induction of µ-lipophagy, which by causing LDs to be digested provides precursors for mitochondrial energy production in the absence of glucose.
source: A key survival promoting role of AMPK under acute GR that we observed was the induction of µ-lipophagy, which by causing LDs to be digested provides precursors for mitochondrial energy production in the absence of glucose.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that AMPK is required for µ-lipophagy and that µ-lipophagy is associated with increased oxygen consumption and ATP production.

claim: There is a fundamental plasticity in the regulation and function of core autophagy components under different starvation conditions.
source: Thus, there appears to be a fundamental plasticity in the regulation and function of core autophagy components under different starvation conditions- with Atg14p directing bulk autophagy under TOR inhibition, but driving µ-lipophagy under AMPK activation (i.e. acute GR).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Atg14p has different roles under different starvation conditions.

claim: Atg14p directs bulk autophagy under TOR inhibition.
source: Thus, there appears to be a fundamental plasticity in the regulation and function of core autophagy components under different starvation conditions- with Atg14p directing bulk autophagy under TOR inhibition, but driving µ-lipophagy under AMPK activation (i.e. acute GR).
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that Atg14p is required for autophagy under nitrogen starvation and rapamycin treatment.

claim: Atg14p drives µ-lipophagy under AMPK activation (acute GR).
source: Thus, there appears to be a fundamental plasticity in the regulation and function of core autophagy components under different starvation conditions- with Atg14p directing bulk autophagy under TOR inhibition, but driving µ-lipophagy under AMPK activation (i.e. acute GR).
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that Atg14p is required for µ-lipophagy under acute GR.

claim: Atg14p shifts its distribution under different starvation regimens to facilitate different autophagic pathways.
source: Thus, Atg14p shifts its distribution under different starvation regimens to facilitate different autophagic pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Atg14p localizes to ERES under gradual GR/rapamycin and to the vacuole under acute GR.

claim: The physical interaction between Snf1p and Atg14p could help stabilize Snf1p against proteasomal degradation.
source: What causes Atg14p's redistribution from ERES/cytosol onto the vacuolar surface upon acute GR remains unclear but could be related to the physical interaction between Snf1p and Atg14p that we observed arising under these conditions. This interaction could help stabilize Snf1p against proteasomal degradation (occurring when TOR is inactivated or under glucose-rich conditions) and may signal Atg14p's redistribution from ERES onto the vacuole.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: The physical interaction between Snf1p and Atg14p may signal Atg14p's redistribution from ERES onto the vacuole.
source: What causes Atg14p's redistribution from ERES/cytosol onto the vacuolar surface upon acute GR remains unclear but could be related to the physical interaction between Snf1p and Atg14p that we observed arising under these conditions. This interaction could help stabilize Snf1p against proteasomal degradation (occurring when TOR is inactivated or under glucose-rich conditions) and may signal Atg14p's redistribution from ERES onto the vacuole.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Atg14p's role on the vacuole surface is likely related to the formation of large Lo domains.
source: Atg14p's role on the vacuole surface is likely related to the formation of large Lo domains (see Figure 9), which are proposed to function as entry portals for LD uptake into the vacuole (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Atg14p is required for Lo domain formation and a citation to prior literature.

claim: LDs dock exclusively at Lo domains on the vacuole surface.
source: We observed that LDs dock exclusively at Lo domains on the vacuole surface.
evidence: This is supported by the confocal imaging data showing LDs in Lo domains.

claim: Atg14p helps stabilize/form large Lo domains.
source: That Atg14p helps stabilize/form these large Lo domains is supported by our findings that: (1) Atg14p localizes on the rims of these domains, (2) deletion of Atg14p abolishes the domains, and (3) conditions that prevent Atg14p from redistributing onto the vacuole (including deletion of SNF1, rapamycin treatment, or gradual GR) diminishes the Lo domains and results in no LD uptake into the vacuole.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Atg14p localization, the effect of atg14Δ on Lo domains, and the effect of conditions that prevent Atg14p redistribution.

claim: LDs play other roles during starvation than simply providing an alternate carbon source for energy production when glucose is absent, including supplying lipids for bulk autophagy and serving as a reservoir for stress-induced excess/damaged lipids.
source: LDs play other role(s) during starvation than simply providing an alternate carbon source for energy production when glucose is absent. This includes supplying lipids for bulk autophagy (Dupont et al., 2014; Shpilka et al., 2015), and serving as a reservoir for stress-induced excess/damaged lipids (Velázquez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: These other LD functions are not sufficient for cells to survive long-term under nutrient starvation unless LD consumption is occurring by µ-lipophagy.
source: While important, these other LD functions are not sufficient for cells to survive long-term under nutrient starvation unless LD consumption is occurring by µ-lipophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that cells without µ-lipophagy have shortened lifespans.

claim: In glucose-starved cells in which µ-lipophagy is absent, less energy is produced relative to cells engaged in µ-lipophagy, and cells survive only short-term.
source: Evidence supporting this came from our findings that in glucose-starved cells in which µ-lipophagy is absent (i.e. atg14Δ cells, snf1Δ cells, cells under gradual GR, or rapamycin-treated cells), less energy is produced relative to cells engaged in µ-lipophagy, and cells survive only short-term.
evidence: This is supported by the ATP level and cell survival data.

claim: µ-lipophagy is more significant than mitophagy or pexophagy for cell longevity under starvation by acute GR conditions.
source: That µ-lipophagy is more significant than either of these for cell longevity under starvation by acute GR conditions was suggested by our findings that in mitophagy-deficient (e.g. atg32Δ and atg33Δ) cells or pexophagy-deficient atg11Δ cells, µ-lipophagy and long-term survival still occurred.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that mitophagy- and pexophagy-deficient cells still survive under acute GR.

claim: AMPK and vacuole-associated Atg14p activities play critical roles in cell survival under acute GR by triggering µ-lipophagy.
source: In summary, our data demonstrate that AMPK and vacuole-associated Atg14p activities play critical roles in cell survival under acute GR by triggering µ-lipophagy (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The key step for µ-lipophagy is early onset AMPK signaling caused by acute GR.
source: The key step for this process is early onset AMPK signaling caused by acute GR.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that AMPK activation is required for µ-lipophagy.

claim: AMPK signaling leads to the relocation of Atg14p from ERES to the vacuole.
source: This leads to the relocation of Atg14p, which also physically interacts with AMPK/Snf1p, from ERES to the vacuole.
evidence: This is supported by the confocal imaging and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: On the vacuole surface, Atg14p initiates µ-lipophagy by working in conjunction with Atg6p and other core autophagy machinery.
source: On the vacuole surface, Atg14p initiates µ-lipophagy by working in conjunction with Atg6p and other core autophagy machinery.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that both Atg14p and Atg6p are required for µ-lipophagy.

claim: Through their cooperative roles in promoting µ-lipophagy, AMPK, Atg14p, Atg6p, and other core autophagy machinery enable yeast cells undergoing acute GR to dramatically extend their lifespans relative to cells experiencing gradual GR or rapamycin treatment.
source: Through their cooperative roles in promoting µ-lipophagy, these components enable yeast cells undergoing acute GR to dramatically extend their lifespans relative to cells experiencing gradual GR or rapamycin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by the cell survival data.

claim: Cells only preserved Snf1p activity and stimulated µ-lipophagy when Snf1p was activated as a consequence of acute glucose depletion.
source: Cells only preserved Snf1p activity and stimulated µ-lipophagy when Snf1p was activated as a consequence of acute glucose depletion (no similar response occurred when TOR was deactivated by amino acid loss or rapamycin treatment).
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot and flux assay data.

claim: AMPK activation selectively promotes autophagic recycling of stored carbon-energy sources (e.g. lipids), while TOR inhibition activates autophagy pathways leading to recycling of nitrogen sources (i.e. digestion of protein-enriched compartments).
source: This supports the notion that AMPK activation selectively promotes autophagic recycling of stored carbon-energy sources (e.g. lipids), while TOR inhibition activates autophagy pathways leading to recycling of nitrogen sources (i.e. digestion of protein-enriched compartments).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing different autophagy pathways under AMPK activation versus TOR inhibition.

claim: Under different nutrient stresses, yeast cells choose distinct autophagic pathways for digestion of different substrates (e.g. lipids versus amino acids) to optimize cell metabolism and survival.
source: Thus, under different nutrient stresses, yeast cells choose distinct autophagic pathways for digestion of different substrates (e.g. lipids versus amino acids) to optimize cell metabolism and survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing different autophagy pathways under different starvation conditions.

claim: These findings are germane to understanding cell survival mechanisms under different starvation regimens and should be relevant for clarifying cellular mechanisms for abnormal metabolic processes associated with cancer, obesity and aging.
source: Given the shared cellular machinery between yeast and other organisms, these findings are germane to understanding cell survival mechanisms under different starvation regimens and should be relevant for clarifying cellular mechanisms for abnormal metabolic processes associated with cancer, obesity and aging.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.
